strengths: Highly original and theoretically elegant concept of utilizing the extended observability subspace and its Grassmannian geometry to regularize State Space Models (SSMs) in a representation-invariant (P-equivalence) way.

Excellent computational optimization, reducing the Sylvester equation complexity from O(n^3) to O(n^2) by taking advantage of the diagonal structure of structured SSMs, which yields a substantial FLOP reduction.

Strong empirical performance on multiple challenging benchmarks (ImageNet-R, CIFAR-100, Caltech-256), demonstrating significant reductions in the forgetting measure (FM) and improvements in average accuracy (AA) under the exemplar-free class-incremental setting.

Great versatility and compatibility; the proposed regularization is successfully integrated as a plug-and-play module with multiple replay-based (ER, LUCIR, X-DER) and prompt-based (L2P) continual learning methods.
Extensive theoretical analysis and proofs provided in the appendix, establishing distance equivalences on the infinite Grassmannian.
weaknesses: The extension to the time-varying S6 model (Mamba) requires averaging the state transition parameters over sequence dimensions to apply LTI-based observability. This simplification essentially ignores the input-dependent dynamic 'selection' mechanism of Mamba during regularization, which could limit its efficacy on highly dynamic sequence modeling tasks.

To overcome numerical instability due to ill-conditioned matrices, the authors employ a noisy rank-1 approximation of the observability matrix. While mathematically tractable and empirically justified, discarding the remaining dimensions of the subspace is a heuristic that may lose finer-grained structural information.

The method requires breaking the optimized selective scan CUDA kernel ('scan-breaking') to save and recompute intermediate states. The paper lacks a quantitative analysis of the actual computational overhead (training time and peak VRAM) relative to standard parameter-regularization baselines.

The input matrix B is regularized using a simple Frobenius norm in Inf-SSM+ rather than a geometry-aware distance, meaning the system's controllability is not fully integrated into the Riemannian geometry framework.

strengths: Highly original formulation that addresses catastrophic forgetting in State-Space Models (SSMs) from a control-theoretic perspective, specifically regularizing the infinite-horizon behavior encoded in the extended observability subspace.
Strong mathematical grounding, nicely bridging the invariance of the observability subspace under P-equivalence with distance metrics on the infinite-dimensional Grassmannian.
Excellent computational efficiency design, reducing the complexity of solving the Sylvester equation from O(n^3) to O(n^2) by leveraging the diagonal structure of modern structured SSMs.

Extensive empirical validation demonstrating that the proposed Inf-SSM and Inf-SSM+ outperform traditional regularization and distillation baselines by a wide margin in Exemplar-Free Class Incremental Learning (EFCIL), while showing strong compatibility when integrated into replay-based and prompt-based CL methods.
The manuscript is exceptionally well-organized, offering rigorous proofs, comprehensive ablation studies, and highly detailed implementation parameters in the appendix.
weaknesses: The adaptation to S6/Mamba (Section 3.4) relies on averaging time-varying matrices over the sequence dimension to form a time-invariant approximation. While empirically effective, this approximation collapses the dynamic, input-dependent nature of S6, which is its core strength.

The rank-1 approximation of the observability matrix used in the simplified distance formulation (Section D.5) is highly heuristic. More theoretical analysis is needed to explain why a rank-1 approximation is sufficient to represent the principal angles without losing critical sequence modeling details.

The method has a 'scan-breaking' limitation as noted in Appendix E. Recomputing and saving intermediate states outside the optimized CUDA scan kernel increases VRAM usage and training time. Providing quantitative wall-clock training time overhead comparisons in the main paper would be beneficial.

The evaluation is limited to vision-based SSMs (Vim). Since SSMs are widely celebrated for long-range 1D sequence and language modeling, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness on a language or sequential continual learning benchmark would greatly broaden its impact.

strengths: Highly original theoretical framework that leverages the mathematical structure of State-Space Models (SSMs). Applying the P-equivalence orbit invariance and the extended observability subspace on the infinite Grassmannian to mitigate catastrophic forgetting is a novel and elegant approach.

Excellent computational optimization. Successfully reducing the complexity of solving the Sylvester equation from O(n^3) to O(n^2) by exploiting the diagonal structure of modern SSMs makes the infinite-horizon regularization practically feasible.

Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple standard datasets (ImageNet-R, CIFAR-100, Caltech-256) demonstrating significant improvements over flagship exemplar-free continual learning baselines (EwC, SI, MAS, LwF).

Versatile and modular design. The paper demonstrates that Inf-SSM can easily be integrated into replay-based and prompt-based CL methods (such as ER, LUCIR, X-DER, and L2P-R), yielding consistent performance gains.
weaknesses: The handling of the input parameter B (representing system controllability) is theoretically less elegant than the treatment of (A, C). While Inf-SSM+ attempts to regularize B using a simple Frobenius norm, this penalty lacks the orbit-invariance properties of the observability-based loss.

Averaging the time-varying parameters of selective SSMs (S6) along the sequence dimension to form time-invariant approximations (A_tilde, C_tilde) is mathematically necessary but might oversimplify the core selective mechanism that gives Mamba/Vim its expressive power.

The practical 'scan-breaking' limitation. Extracting intermediate state matrices A, B, and C during the forward pass breaks the optimized CUDA scan kernels of modern SSM backbones, which increases VRAM footprint and training latency.

High sensitivity and large variance in the optimal regularization hyperparameters (e.g., the lambda parameter in Tables 9 and 10 ranges from 10^4 to over 10^6 depending on the dataset), indicating that deployment on new datasets might require extensive hyperparameter tuning.

strengths: The paper introduces a highly original, geometry-aware regularization method (Inf-SSM) specifically tailored to the unique system-theoretic structure of State Space Models (SSMs), filling an important gap in continual learning for selective recurrence architectures.

Strong theoretical motivation leveraging the extended observability subspace on the infinite Grassmannian, ensuring that the regularization is invariant to P-equivalence (functionally identical state-space parameterizations).

Elegant solution to computational bottlenecks: exploiting the diagonal structure of contemporary SSMs to reduce Sylvester equation complexity from O(n^3) to O(n^2) and introducing a stable rank-1 approximation that reduces distance computation time by over 99%.

Extensive empirical validation showing consistent and significant improvements (up to ~8.3% average accuracy gain and ~9.3% reduction in forgetting) when integrated into representative continual learning baselines on multiple benchmarks (ImageNet-R, CIFAR-100, Caltech-256) and backbones (Vim-small, Vim-tiny).
Excellent writing and exceptionally thorough appendix containing detailed mathematical proofs, comprehensive implementation details, and multiple additional studies (e.g., CKD states analysis).
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees of invariance are derived under Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) assumptions, whereas modern architectures (like Vim and Mamba) are time-varying (selective). Although the authors handle this via spatial/temporal averaging (Section 3.3), the formal connection between the averaged LTI-like system and the true time-varying dynamics is somewhat heuristic.

The practical implementation of extracting intermediate states for regularization breaks the optimized CUDA scan of SSMs ('scan-breaking'), leading to increased training time and VRAM usage. While correctable via future custom CUDA kernels, this remains a current limitation for practical scaling.

The simplified distance formula (Eq. 33) models the observability matrix as a noisy rank-1 matrix because the Gram matrices are ill-conditioned. It would be beneficial to discuss if this rank-1 assumption drops crucial high-order dynamical information in complex long-range tasks.

strengths: The paper introduces a highly novel perspective for Continual Learning (CL) in State-Space Models (SSMs) by leveraging system-theoretic properties, specifically P-equivalence and the infinite-dimensional Grassmannian of observability subspaces. This is a significant departure from standard parameter-regularization methods that treat SSM weights as generic neural network parameters.

The mathematical formulation is elegant and computationally optimized. By exploiting the diagonal structure of modern SSMs (like S4D, Mamba, Vim), the authors successfully reduce the computational complexity of solving the Sylvester equation from $O(n^3)$ to $O(n^2)$, enabling a 100x FLOPS reduction for the metric computation.

Extensive empirical validation is conducted across standard CL benchmarks (ImageNet-R, CIFAR-100, Caltech-256) in both 5-task and 10-task scenarios. Inf-SSM consistently yields significant improvements in final accuracy, average incremental accuracy, and forgetting rate when integrated into diverse CL baselines (e.g., ER, LUCIR, X-DER, CLFD, L2P-R).

The paper is exceptionally well-written, with rigorous mathematical proofs provided in the appendix and comprehensive ablation studies (such as different model sizes like Vim-tiny, and the effect of including B in the regularization).
weaknesses: The extension to time-varying SSMs (S6/Mamba) requires computing the observability distance for each token position in the sequence of length $\tau$. Although averaging across the channel dimension $o$ makes it more tractable, this 'scan-breaking' process still introduces noticeable VRAM and training time overhead. A more detailed discussion or empirical scaling analysis of this sequence-length overhead during training would strengthen the paper.

The $O(n^2)$ optimization relies heavily on the diagonal structure of the state transition matrix $A$. While diagonal parameterization is common in modern SSMs, for general non-diagonal SSMs, one would have to resort to the $O(n^3)$ Bartels-Stewart algorithm, which might limit the generalizability of the efficient version of Inf-SSM.

strengths: Highly Original and Geometric Perspective: Uniquely addresses catastrophic forgetting in State-Space Models (SSMs) by focusing on their state-space representation and geometry (specifically P-equivalence and the Grassmannian of observability subspaces) rather than treating them as generic flat weights.

Elegant Theoretical Foundation: Excellent formulation using the infinite-dimensional Grassmannian and the extended observability matrix. The connection to Sylvester equations and the invariant properties under P-equivalence are mathematically rigorous and well-explained.

Impressive Complexity Reduction: Cleverly exploits the diagonal structure of modern structured SSMs (e.g., S4D, Mamba) to reduce the computational complexity of solving the Sylvester equation from O(n^3) to O(n^2), enabling a fast and practical implementation (up to 100x FLOP reduction).

Comprehensive Experiments: Evaluated extensively on several competitive CL benchmarks (ImageNet-R, CIFAR-100, Caltech-256) with a Vim-small backbone. It demonstrates substantial improvements when integrated into existing CL baselines (both replay and exemplar-free) and consistently outperforms standard EFCIL methods.
weaknesses: Rank-1 Approximation for Distance: The simplified distance metric on the Grassmannian (Eq. 33) assumes that the observability matrix can be approximated as rank-1. While the authors justify this with a Monte Carlo correlation study, this approximation collapses the n-dimensional state dynamics into a single dominant direction, which might lose fine-grained temporal characteristics in complex sequential tasks.

Heuristics for Non-LTI (Selective) SSMs: Modern SSMs like Mamba (S6) are input-dependent and time-varying. To apply the LTI-based observability formulation, the authors resort to averaging the state parameters over the sequence length and outer channels. Although empirically effective, this step is a heuristic approximation that deviates from the clean mathematical formulation of LTI systems.

Scan-Breaking Overhead: The implementation requires extracting intermediate states during the forward pass, which breaks the highly optimized fused CUDA scans of Mamba/Vim. This 'scan-breaking' nature increases the training time and memory overhead during training, which limits its immediate plug-and-play efficiency without custom kernel development.
